To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the pH-dependent interaction potential between an object with smeared-out charges (e.g., a DNA molecule) and a membrane with mobile charged lipds depends on the membrane fluidity; and that (ii) the membrane fluidity has a considerable impact on adsorption behavior and distribution of surface ions.

the pH-dependent interaction between DNA and a charged membrane is strongly influenced by the in-plane mobility and the charge state of the membrane surface groups, and that the pH-dependent charge regulation of biological membranes is an important factor in the understanding of the DNA-membrane interaction.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and application of a general theory of the interaction of a DNA or protein with a membrane that takes into account the pH-dependent charge regulation and the in-plane mobility and fluidity of membrane surface groups.
the development and application of theoretical methods for the description and analysis of the interaction of charged biomolecules with model membranes.
the development and application of theoretical methods for modeling the interaction between charged objects and charged surfaces in the presence of mobile counterions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
membrane fluidity is a key parameter for the interaction between DNA and membranes.
, at short distances, the membrane fluidity can be of great importance for the interaction between a DNA and a model membrane.
the charge regulation mechanism is crucial for the understanding of the DNA/membrbrane interaction and that the pH and the membrane fluidity can play a significant role in this interaction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pH-dependent interaction between DNA and a charged membrane can have a strong dependence on the in-plane mobility and the charge density of the membrane surface groups.

, for biological membranes, the pH and the in-plane mobility are both important for the charge regulation of the membrane and that the pH dependence of the interaction between a charged object, such as a DNA molecule, and such a membrane is more complex than previously thought.
we have developed a new theoretical approach to the calculation of the mean-field interaction between charged objects and biological membranes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when modeling charged objects interacting with biological membranes, one has to take into account both the pH-dependent chemical and the in-plane mobility-induced charge regulation mechanisms.
the charge-regulating mechanisms of biological membranes can be very complex and need to be taken into account when modeling the electrostatics of membrane systems.

, in the case of biological membranes with mobile lipids, one cannot use the usual boundary condition at the surface that is appropriate only in the case of charge regulation through the chemical equilibrium.
